articles.title: Refurbished tablets are having a moment, and retailers are noticing
articles.subtitle: Certified refurb programs are getting more prominent shelf space
articles.excerpt: Certified refurbished tablets are seeing a sales bump as buyers look for a middle ground between new prices and uncertain secondhand listings.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Certified refurbished programs used to be a niche corner of a retailer's site. Several major sellers now report refurbished tablets are among their fastest-growing categories by unit volume.
Why now
Buyers increasingly cite battery health guarantees and standardized grading as the deciding factor over cheaper, ungraded secondhand listings from individual sellers.
Retailers say return rates on certified refurbished units are now close to those of new devices, a gap that was much wider just a few years ago.

articles.title: The kids-mode tablet market is more competitive than it looks
articles.subtitle: A crowded shelf of near-identical devices is hiding real differences
articles.excerpt: At a glance, most kids tablets look interchangeable. A closer look at parental controls and content filtering shows real gaps between them.
articles.author: admin

content.text: At a glance, most kids tablets look interchangeable: a bright case, a simplified interface, and a marketing claim about screen time limits. A closer look at how parental controls actually work shows real differences.
What actually differs between them

items: Whether content filtering happens on-device or requires a constant connection
How granular screen-time scheduling actually is
Whether app purchases can be fully blocked, not just flagged

content.text: Several models marketed specifically for younger children still allow access to the full app store behind a PIN that's trivial for an elementary-age kid to guess.

articles.title: Why some artists still prefer a $50 tablet over a $1,000 one
articles.subtitle: Pressure sensitivity isn't the only thing that matters at the easel
articles.excerpt: Professional illustrators explain why a budget drawing tablet sometimes beats a flagship device for their actual workflow.
articles.author: admin

content.text: It would be easy to assume every professional illustrator reaches for the most expensive tablet available. In practice, several told us they keep a sub-$50 drawing tablet in rotation for specific parts of their workflow.
The case for the cheap one
A dedicated, screen-less drawing tablet paired with a large monitor avoids the parallax and glare issues that come with drawing directly on a glass display, at a fraction of the cost.
For rough sketching and thumbnails specifically, several artists said the lack of a screen actually helped them avoid over-polishing early drafts.

articles.title: Stylus latency finally got good enough to stop noticing
articles.subtitle: The lag that used to make handwriting feel artificial is mostly gone
articles.excerpt: For years, stylus input on tablets had just enough lag to feel slightly artificial. The newest generation has largely closed that gap.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Earlier tablet styluses had just enough input lag to feel slightly artificial, especially for handwriting, where your eye expects the ink to appear the instant the tip touches down.
The numbers behind the feel
Reported latency on the newest displays has dropped to roughly a third of what flagship tablets shipped with five years ago, a gap most users reported as no longer noticeable in side-by-side testing.
Note-taking app developers say the improvement has meaningfully changed how comfortable long handwritten sessions feel, particularly for users switching from paper.

articles.title: Is the tablet finally replacing the laptop for students
articles.subtitle: A semester-long experiment says almost
articles.excerpt: We tracked how a group of college students used tablets as their primary computer for a full term, and the results were mixed but promising.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Overview
We tracked how a group of college students used tablets as their primary computer for a full term, and the results were mixed but promising.
The details

A semester-long experiment says almost. We tracked how a group of college students used tablets as their primary computer for a full term, and by the end, 70% said they didn't miss a laptop for note-taking or reading.
bold: 70% said they didn't miss a laptop

content.text: The friction point was consistent across the group: spreadsheet-heavy coursework and long-form writing assignments over roughly 2,000 words were where a physical keyboard and multi-window support were still missed most.
What helped

items: A keyboard case used for more than half of all sessions
Cloud storage syncing automatically across a phone and tablet

content.text: Our take

It's an encouraging sign for where the category is headed next, even if not every question has been answered yet — heavier coursework like video editing or coding classes wasn't part of this particular group.
